question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = xe^{xy}-2\cos y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $(1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(1,0\right) &= 1\cdot e^{1\cdot 0}-2\cos 0 \\[3pt] &= 1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1\\[3pt] &= -1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(1,0)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\[5pt] z - (-1) &= (-1)y \\[5pt] z &= -y - 1 \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = 1 \\[3pt] z = -y -1 \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ Given that the point $P\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_x = \sqrt 2\sin(2y)\cos y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \sqrt 2 \sin\left(2\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\cos \dfrac{\pi}{4} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt 2\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\[3pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= f_x\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)(x-1) \\[3pt] z - 0&= 1 (x-1) \\[3pt] z &= x-1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{4},0\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ z = x - 1 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $y = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = x - 1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 0, 1, 0 \rangle \times \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=-\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle -1,0,-1 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, since $\langle -1,0,-1 \rangle$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-\langle -1,0,-1 \rangle = \langle 1,0,1 \rangle$ is also parallel to it.

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P\left(\sqrt{2},2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = -\dfrac{2x^2+y}{y^3} $, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P\left(\sqrt{2},2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y} \Bigg|_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(\sqrt{2},2\right) &= -\dfrac{2(\sqrt{2})^2+2}{2^3}\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4+2}{8} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{4} \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - z|_{(\sqrt{2},2)} &= \dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}\Bigg |_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\[5pt] z - \dfrac{1}{2} &= -\dfrac{3}{4}(y-2) \\[5pt] z &= -\dfrac{3}{4}y+{2} \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(\sqrt{2},2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x = \sqrt{2} \\[5pt] z = -\dfrac{3}{4}y+{2} \end{cases} \]

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = x + 2x\ln(xy) + \dfrac 1y $, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= 2 + 2(2)\ln\left(2\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{({1}/{2})} \\[5pt] &= 2 + 4\ln 1 + 2\\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= f_y\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(y-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 4 \left(y-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 4y-2 \\[5pt] z &= 4y - 1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(2,\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = 2 \\ z = 4y - 1 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = 2,$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = 4y - 1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,4,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, 4, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{j} + 4\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 0,1,4\rangle \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\langle 0,1,4\rangle.$

question.text: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Given that the point $P\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1,0\right)$ lies on $C$, and that $f_y = 2\sin(xy) -\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi }{2}y\right) $, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.explanation:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)&= 2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot 1 \right) - \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot 1\right) \\[5pt] &= 2\cdot 1 - 0 \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align*}

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

\begin{align*} z - f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right) &= f_y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)\left(y-1\right) \\[5pt] z - 0 &= 2 \left(y-1\right) \\[5pt] z &= 2y-2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1,0\right)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes: \[ \begin{cases} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\[5pt] z = 2y - 2 \end{cases} \]

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle.$

  • For the plane $z = 2y - 2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 0,2,-1 \rangle.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 & = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, 2, -1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \begin{array}{|ccc|} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \end{array} \\[5pt] &=\mathbf{j} + 2\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \langle 0,1,2\rangle \end{align*}

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\langle 0,1,2\rangle.$
